entry.title: India-EU trade pact needs investment safeguards to fulfil its promise
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India-EU trade pact needs investment safeguards to fulfil its promiseIndia-EU trade pact needs investment safeguards to fulfil its promise

A trade agreement two decades in the making could pave the way for a defining partnership of the century

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Dammu Ravi6 min read Last Updated : Nov 18 2026 | 9:44 PM ISTNext month, Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be in Brussels for the formal signing of the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) on December 15-16, following nearly two decades of negotiations.  For India, this will truly be the mother of all FTAs. For the first time, it is entering into a comprehensive and highly ambitious agreement, with a scope and coverage never seen before in its trade agreements. The FTA has 20 chapters, including subjects India has never previously agreed to include in its trade deals, such as digital trade, gender, labour, environment and sustainability, government procurement, and intellectual property, with strong provisions of cooperation in these areas. Its significance should be seen against the backdrop of the growing unilateralism, with huge implications for global economic stability. India and the European Union (EU) are two large democracies with a combined gross domestic product of over $24 trillion — the EU at $20 trillion and India at $4 trillion. Together, they account for nearly one-fourth of humanity bound by shared democratic values and the rule of law. Leaders on both sides are upbeat about its potential to take the India-EU Strategic Partnership to the next level.  Expectations are high that the FTA will deliver mutually beneficial outcomes, but for it to happen, perceptual gaps on both sides must be narrowed.  Trade beyond binaries: Industry on both sides believe bilateral goods and services trade, worth $136.54 billion and $83.10 billion respectively, could double within a decade under the FTA. India currently enjoys surpluses of $15.17 billion in goods and $10 billion in services trade. The EU’s cumulative foreign direct investment in India since 2000 stands at $117.4 billion, with total investment stock, including equity and portfolio, exceeding $300 billion. About 6,000 EU companies are operating in the country. India’s cumulative investment in the EU stands at about $50 billion during the same period, with about 1,500 companies operating there.  However, viewing trade through the binary lens of deficits or surpluses risks making it a victim of popular concern. Global trade moves through a complex web of supply chains that hinges on facilitation. Trade facilitation on both ends involves alignment of tariffs and non-tariff barriers. The breadth of the FTA is a true reflection of their commitment to address these barriers and the irritants that impede trade.  Investment is the linchpin: Another perceptual gap that needs closing is in investment. Trade and investment are intimately linked. Trade is an integr-ated activity in which goods, services, investment, tec­-hnology and finance interplay. Framing investment rules must take these linkages into account.  Yet, this is also the FTA’s shortcoming. The FTA does not contain a comprehensive investment protection chapter. Investment protection is being pursued separately through a bilateral investment treaty (BIT), which is still under negotiation. Until that treaty is concluded, the FTA will remain incomplete in the very area that matters most for long-term investor confidence. A mutually agreed investment framework linked to the FTA is crucial for attracting EU investment under our production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme, particularly in the green energy sector. This should cover the entire value chain, including the manufacture of components and technology transfer in polysilicon, wafers, electrolysers, wind turbines, green ammonia and battery storage, as well as grid and transmission infrastructure.  Equipment for the green energy transition must be manufactured at scale, mostly by Indian micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), to meet ever-growing energy demand. Its strategic dimension must be seen against the backdrop of weaponisation of dependencies and concentration of supply chains, which can be detrimental to both India and the EU.  A novel way to settle disputes: Our fear of international arbitration in foreign investment has restrained our approach thus far, a significant factor behind the provisions for domestic remedies in our Model BIT of 2015, which is currently under revision. For the EU, investment protection is important, but even more significant for its industry is the promotion and facilitation of investment to ensure transparency and predictability in taxation, approvals and time-bound redress.  It cuts both ways. As emerging economies are now investing robustly in developed countries, this enhanced two-way flow of investment is one reason why most developed countries are now seeking to move away from the Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) provision, which had been a major concern of developing countries.  The EU has made a strong pitch for a State-to-State Dispute Settlement (SSDS) mechanism in its framework BIT. It opens up options for diplomatic engagement and trade-offs, just as India and the US traded off their disputes pending before the WTO during Prime Minister Modi’s visit to the US in February 2025. The EU’s suggestion for SSDS in the bilateral investment treaty with India merits closer examination, given that Indian companies too need protection as they invest in European brands.  The green bargain: The EU views India as an important strategic partner beyond trade. It sees India’s choices as having global consequences in many ways, especially in the climate arena. It wants India to align its policies with its climate objectives as a win-win for both sides. It seeks to link India’s industrial policy, energy security, supply chains and critical minerals with the EU’s decarbonisation goals.  Horizon Europe could help upscale research & development initiatives in a collaborative way. The EU believes that achieving its climate-neutral economy, with a carbon reduction target of up to 90 per cent by 2040, needs strong partners like India to find solutions together. It thus sees India not as an option, but as an imperative.  The EU’s desire to initiate a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) dialogue with India should be seen in this context. Overcoming the perceptual gap here is challenging.  Most Indian companies view CBAM’s complex carbon pricing mechanism as a deliberate tool to deny market access, since its imposition is incompatible with WTO rules without a Special and Differential Treatment (S&DT) carve-out for developing countries or recognition of the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).  Much depends on how the EU can assuage the genuine fears of Indian industry. The €500 million fund to support decarbonisation initiatives of Indian industry is a good beginning, but it needs to be aligned with India’s green tax initiative to make it enduring. Blended financing and green funds of the EU can be tapped for collaborative, bankable projects in green ancillary infrastructure.  A Viksit Bharat 2047 catalyst: The significance of the FTA should thus be seen in the broader context of two large entities coming together to forge a partnership that will be transformative on the global stage.  Institutional support, either through Invest India or NITI Aayog, could provide a useful hand-holding role on facilitation issues. For India, an investment framework embedded in the India-EU FTA can be an effective catalyst for driving Viksit Bharat 2047. If implemented with vision and trust, this FTA can become not just a trade deal, but a defining partnership for the century.
The writer is former secretary (economic relations), Ministry of External Affairs, and writes on trade, development, and geoeconomics     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Delhi's toxic air demands citizen accountability, year-round action
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Delhi's toxic air demands citizen accountability, year-round actionDelhi's toxic air demands citizen accountability, year-round action

Nobody is coming to rescue Delhi from itself. Its people must decide whether they and their children deserve to breathe

premium

The Air Quality Life Index estimates that the average Delhi resident loses 8.2 years of life to fine particulate pollution above the World Health Organization’s guidelines

Amit Kapoor5 min read Last Updated : Nov 18 2026 | 9:52 PM ISTOn the night of November 8, as the last Diwali crackers went off, private sensors reporting on the American scale logged air quality index (AQI) readings above 1,700 for Delhi and above 2,000 in some neighbourhoods. Meanwhile, the official index, which by design stops at 500, had 20 of its 59 stations in the severe band by 10 pm.  We fumigate granaries to rid them of rats and spray fields to rid them of locusts, and every winter Delhi now does to its own people what it would otherwise reserve for pests, sealing them inside a filthy chamber of smoke and dust and calling it winter. The Air Quality Life Index estimates that the average Delhi resident loses 8.2 years of life to fine particulate pollution above the World Health Organization’s guidelines. Across India, the State of Global Air report attributed two million deaths in 2023 to polluted air, up from 1.4 million in 2000. Primary schools moved to hybrid classes on November 7, and a generation is growing up believing that a mask and a sealed window are what childhood looks like in the national capital.  Those who govern us have turned the crisis, and even its numbers, into a contest of narratives. For years, the blame fell on Punjab’s farmers. Then official counts of farm fires began to drop — by more than 90 per cent between 2020 and 2025. Yet a National Aeronautics and Space Administration-affiliated scientist estimates that Punjab and Haryana saw 34,000 fires between October 1 and November 9, compared with the 4,459 officially counted in Punjab by November 8. This is because burning has moved to the late afternoon, after the satellites have passed overhead.  Whatever the true count, the filth is largely our own. This year’s review of a decade of studies by the Commission for Air Quality Management’s expert panel traces 27 per cent of Delhi’s winter PM2.5 to particles formed from gases such as sulphur dioxide, 23 per cent to transport, 20 per cent to the burning of biomass and waste, 15 per cent to dust, and 9 per cent to industry and power plants.  Responsibility has been passed from desk to desk at every level of authority until nobody holds it. The National Clean Air Programme has released ₹16,824 crore to 130 cities since 2019, yet 117 of them still breached the national standard for coarse particles in 2025-26. By the middle of 2025, Delhi had spent only ₹13.94 crore of the ₹42.69 crore it had received under the scheme. In July 2025, the environment ministry exempted 78 per cent of the country’s coal plants from installing units that strip sulphur from their smoke, and the exempted plants now account for 81 per cent of the sulphur dioxide emitted by coal plants within 300 km of the capital. Each of these decisions came with its reasons, and together they amount to a surrender. Who will answer for this? The Supreme Court has been issuing orders on Delhi’s air since a petition was filed in 1985, commissions and action plans have multiplied, and no god is going to come down to clear the sky. The answers, therefore, will have to come from us. A civilisation that never tires of reminding the world of its antiquity once wrote municipal rules into the Arthashastra, fining anyone who threw dirt on the street an eighth of a pana and doubling the fine on the king’s road. Its heirs now foul the air of their capital and wait for the wind to change. Pride in that past will not clean a single breath, and a people that cannot protect its children’s lungs is working its way towards extinction, however old its civilisation.  Delhi needs a radical awakening of conscience, in those who hold office and in those of us who elect them, and a new social contract between the two that treats clean air as the first duty of the state in every month of the year. Beijing showed what such resolve can achieve when it cut fine particulate pollution by 35.6 per cent between 2013 and 2017. The United Nations Environment Programme’s review credits the largest share of that improvement to replacing coal in boilers and homes and 23 per cent to cuts made by its neighbours under a national plan. India, where the Lancet Countdown valued the lives lost to air pollution in 2023 at 13.5 per cent of gross domestic product, can hardly afford to treat clean air as a luxury. Its air quality commission, which can already issue directions to every state around the capital, could hold each state to a binding target. The coal plants around the capital can be made to clean their stacks. Buses and metro feeders can make the private car unnecessary, and fires at landfills can be put out for good. Construction dust can be policed all year, and money already sanctioned can be spent against measured results, with the death toll published as routinely as the AQI. Households carry their share too, in the crackers we light, the waste we burn, and the cars we drive, and voters can make the air an issue that decides elections.  If a single factory poisoned a town this way, we would call it a crime. Spread across governments, industries and households, it still remains one — a slow crime against humanity, with blood on all our hands. Nobody is coming to rescue Delhi from itself, and the choice before its people this winter is whether to go on living like pests in a fumigated city or to decide, at last, that they and their children deserve to breathe. 
The writer is chair, Institute for Competitiveness. X:@kautiliya. With inputs from Meenakshi Ajith     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: European deforestation regulations and the future of Indian exports
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / European deforestation regulations and the future of Indian exportsEuropean deforestation regulations and the future of Indian exports

Indian exporters must strengthen supply-chain traceability to meet EU deforestation rules and protect market access

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ajay Sahai9 min read Last Updated : Nov 18 2026 | 10:08 PM ISTFor a European coffee buyer, the journey of a bean increasingly matters as much as its quality. For a furniture importer, the origin of the timber is becoming part of the purchasing decision. The European Union’s Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) brings these factors into the conditions for market access, with significant implications for Indian suppliers and their international customers. Businesses able to demonstrate where their materials come from can use that transparency to strengthen buyer confidence and win repeat orders.  The scale of the adjustment is substantial. In calendar year 2025 (CY25), the EU’s 27 member-states imported goods worth €2.67 billion from India across tariff lines already listed in the amended regulation. A further €461 million was recorded on lines added from December 30, 2027. These are values of trade on the relevant tariff lines; actual regulatory coverage depends on the product description and, in some cases, the species, material or feedstock. India’s low-risk classification offers a useful starting point, provided suppliers can substantiate the origin and legality of the commodities involved.  The EUDR covers specified products derived from seven commodities — cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood. Covered goods must comply with the relevant laws in the country of production and meet the EU’s deforestation-free requirement, which uses December 31, 2020, as the cut-off date. Wood must also meet a forest degradation requirement. For exporters, this means connecting the finished product to evidence about the land and materials from which it originated. For existing product lines, the rules apply from December 30, 2026, to large and medium operators and to micro and small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation. Most other micro and small operators have until 30 June 2027.  Under Directive 2013/34/EU (the Accounting Directive), as amended by Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2023/2775, a company falls into a category if it does not exceed two of the three criteria (see chart 1). Anything above the medium thresholds is large.    The distinction matters for Indian micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs): A small Indian supplier selling to a large EU importer should prepare for the importer’s December 2026 deadline.  Two measures adopted by the European Commission in July support implementation. A Delegated Act updates and simplifies Annex I, the list of products covered, following stakeholder consultation and public feedback. An Implementing Act sets out how the information system will handle due diligence statements and simplified declarations. The scope update changes the products derived from the seven commodities, without changing the commodity list itself. The Delegated Act removes cattle hides, skins and leather, retreaded tyres, soybeans for sowing, specified articles of vulcanised rubber, conveyor and transmission belts, and aircraft and motor vehicle seats. It adds soluble coffee, certain palm oil derivatives and frozen cattle tongues, with these additions becoming subject to the regulation from December 30, 2027, to give businesses time to prepare. It also clarifies that samples and products used for analysis, examination and testing are outside the scope, and introduces targeted exemptions for specified categories of waste, used and second-hand products, packing material, and products used to manufacture medicinal products.  Where Indian trade is most affected  The existing tariff lines represented about 3.8 per cent of the EU’s €69.63 billion in goods imports from India in 2025. The later additions represented a further 0.7 per cent on the same basis. These national shares, however, can obscure the importance of Europe to individual businesses. A coffee exporter whose orders come predominantly from Europe faces a different adjustment from a diversified tyre manufacturer selling several compounds and product categories.  Rubber, coffee and wood-based products together accounted for about 82 per cent of trade on the existing lines. This concentration points to where common industry support could assist the greatest volume of trade, while careful product classification remains essential within each sector (see chart 2).      Different sectors face different sourcing challenges Rubber and rubber products accounted for €1.03 billion on screened lines. Agricultural and forestry tyres alone represented €634.16 million, although the tariff code does not reveal how much of that trade used covered natural rubber. Tyre treads show why classification at the eight-digit EU customs level matters: The specific code recorded €0.75 million, against €12.38 million for the broader six-digit line. With the 2026 amendment removing retreaded tyres, specified conveyor and transmission belts, and certain other vulcanised rubber articles, exporters can direct compliance spending towards products and materials that remain covered.  Coffee presents a more direct connection between trade and farm-level traceability. Unroasted, non-decaffeinated coffee accounted for €605.54 million of the €605.91 million on existing coffee lines. The immediate task is to trace pooled lots through collection centres and curing works to the contributing farms. Soluble coffee and other coffee extracts and concentrates add €100.11 million on a line applying from December 2027. Processors can use the additional year to map suppliers before purchasing the crop destined for EU production.  Wood, paper and furniture recorded €542.13 million, including €216.13 million in other wooden furniture. For manufacturers buying through several timber dealers, compliance requires a reliable link between finished goods, harvest records and evidence of legality.   Soya accounted for €271.33 million, almost entirely soybean oilcake and other extraction residues.  Among the 2027 additions, specified palm derivatives accounted for €360.83 million in screened trade. Actual coverage depends on feedstock, particularly for chemicals and preparations that can be produced from different oils. The removal of specified cattle hides, skins and leather narrows India’s exposure in that sector, while no 2025 import value was reported on the newly listed frozen cattle tongue line.  What low risk means for buyers and suppliers  India’s low-risk status can simplify an EU importer’s due diligence when the relevant commodity is produced in India and the conditions for simplified treatment are met. It does not remove the need for production-location information, legality records or evidence linking the source to the consignment. The EU importer ordinarily submits the due diligence statement when first placing covered goods on the EU market, using evidence supplied by the Indian exporter. The origin of the commodity is, therefore, crucial. For a tyre manufactured in India using imported natural rubber, the country where the rubber was grown determines its risk classification. The same distinction applies to furniture made with imported timber. Buyers and suppliers need to resolve these questions at the sourcing stage so that a manufacturing location is not mistaken for proof of the underlying commodity’s origin.  Turning preparation into confidence  Exporters should begin with their EU order books. For each product, they should verify the eight-digit EU customs code, covered inputs and required documentation with the importer, then test the process on a live consignment. Lot identifiers should be assigned at collection or receipt, production locations and dates captured, and legality records retained. Material of undocumented origin should be kept out of lots intended for the EU, while manufacturers using imported inputs should secure production data before purchase.  Data arrangements deserve the same attention as physical sourcing. Exporters and buyers should verify who may access farm information, how errors will be corrected and how delays will be handled. A system that works consistently across repeat consignments can help suppliers combine reliable delivery with verifiable sourcing when competing for longer-term contracts. Export facilitation and promotion organisations could make preparation more affordable for smaller firms. A joint advisory could connect EU customs codes with product descriptions and exclusions, supported by sector clinics involving commodity boards and EU importers. Pilot shipments in coffee, tyres and furniture would allow buyer feedback to shape reusable documentation templates and help resolve recurring questions about classification and evidence. Suppliers with verified sourcing records could then be brought into buyer-seller meetings and trade missions, making it easier for European buyers to qualify additional Indian partners.  Government support can address the costs that individual exporters and growers struggle to bear. The TRACE (Trade Regulations, Accreditation and Compliance Enablement) scheme provides reimbursement up to 95 per cent of the costs subject to a ceiling of ~50 lakh for micro and small units and 80 per cent of the cost, with the same ceiling, for medium enterprises. Shared mapping and traceability services, delivered through commodity boards, state agencies and farmer producer organisations, could link farm and plantation records, harvest permissions and lot identifiers through systems able to exchange data. This would reduce repeated information requests and help smaller growers participate. Initial support could focus on clusters where fragmented sourcing creates the highest cost per shipment.  Engagement with the European Commission and member-state authorities should clarify how Indian land and harvest records can demonstrate legality, including which alternative records may be usable where formal documentation is incomplete. This work should proceed alongside the mapping of palm-derived chemical and soluble coffee supply chains for 2027. A joint government-industry review could track growers mapped, pilot lots accepted by buyers, shipment verification costs and resulting repeat business. These measures would reveal where shared services should expand and where firms need assistance with particular buyer requirements.  The export opportunity lies in making traceable sourcing available at commercial scale. A European coffee buyer able to qualify several Indian grower groups, or a furniture buyer able to verify timber across repeat orders, has a stronger basis for placing more business with Indian suppliers. Shared infrastructure can extend that opportunity to smaller exporters and growers, while product-specific trade data can guide investment towards the lines with the strongest growth prospects. For India and its  trading partners, dependable evidence of origin can become an enduring source of commercial confidence. 
 The writer is director general and chief executive officer, Federation of Indian Export Organisations. Views are personal    Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India needs flexible corporate rules that move beyond box-ticking
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India needs flexible corporate rules that move beyond box-tickingIndia needs flexible corporate rules that move beyond box-ticking

India's muscular regulatory regime should make room for alternative governance practices, allowing companies to show a different route to the same goal

premium

Representative image of a corporate board meeting discussing governance and compliance

Amit Tandon5 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:52 PM ISTWhen the Companies Act, 2013, made corporate social responsibility (CSR) a legal obligation, India briefly allowed companies to explain their non-compliance. Boards were to ensure at least 2 per cent of average net profits went to CSR, but a company that fell short faced no penalty. It only had to give its reasons in the board’s report.  That experiment in “comply or explain” is over. Since January 2021, unspent money must be moved to a dedicated account or a government fund, with penalties of up to twice the amount, capped at ₹1 crore. Boards still explain a shortfall, but they need to spend the amount.  The shift fits a pattern. India regulates companies mostly by command. The Companies Act and Sebi (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015 (LODR) prescribe board composition, committees, approval of related-party transactions and disclosures, with penalties for breach. This “comply or else” model offers clear rules and an enforcer with teeth. But rules mean boards learn to satisfy the letter rather than the purpose. A 2014 NSE briefing by Nawshir Mirza and Nirmal Mohanty observed that Indian governance norms were “practised more as rituals in religion than as a genuine pursuit of good governance”.  Mandates also leave regulators few options when a rule meets resistance. In February 2022, weeks before India’s top 500 listed companies had to separate the roles of chairperson and managing director or chief executive officer, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) found only about half had complied. Rather than penalising a large slice of the market, it made the rule voluntary. It could instead have retained the mandate while allowing companies that chose to keep a combined role to explain their reasons to shareholders annually.  Much of the world uses that softer toolkit. Britain adopted “comply or explain” in 1992, following the Cadbury Committee. A code sets out principles and practices. A company may depart from a practice if it explains why publicly, and shareholders, not the regulator, judge the explanation. Variants have followed:  l Apply or explain (South Africa’s King III code, named after Mervyn King, and the Dutch code): Apply the principles and explain how. l Apply and explain (South Africa’s King IV code, UK Stewardship Code): No opt-out; show how each principle is applied. l Report or explain: Publish data, such as sustainability or diversity metrics, or explain why not. l Comply and explain: A mandate plus a narrative, as India’s CSR regime now works. l Opt in or opt out: Sets a default and lets companies choose a different path. Example, the European Union Takeover Directive’s rule that bars boards from frustrating a bid, which member states can opt out of and companies can opt-back in. l If not, why not, is Australia’s version and deserves a closer look.    “If not, why not” works like comply or explain, but differs in emphasis. “Comply or explain” makes compliance the default, so an explanation can read like an excuse. “If not, why not” treats not adopting a recommendation as a decision the board is entitled to make. The Australian Securities Exchange’s principles state that a board that considers a recommendation unsuited to its circumstances is entitled not to adopt it. Companies must give their reasons and say what they do instead. That pushes them to show a different route to the same goal, not just a gap. The approach has lasted two decades, and the draft fifth edition of the principles keeps it.  India has used these tools mainly as a glide path. Besides CSR, Sebi’s rule that large companies raise a quarter of their incremental borrowing through bonds ran on comply or explain for two years before penalties applied. Value-chain disclosures under BRSR Core began as “comply or explain” in 2023 and became voluntary in 2025. The LODR’s list of “discretionary” requirements asks for no explanation at all.  India should ask “if not, why not”.The NSE briefing argued comply or explain needs boards that value good governance, honest explanations and investors who act on them. CSR adds a lesson: Explanation works only where someone has a reason to read it. CSR benefits society rather than shareholders, so investors had little incentive to challenge thin explanations. Today’s domestic funds and insurers, bound by stewardship codes and supported by proxy advisers, are better placed to use it.  Sebi could start by turning the LODR’s “discretionary” norms into “if not, why not” requirements. Companies would report against them, and against others issues such as a separate chairperson, limits on director tenure and board diversity, explaining any departure and the alternative they had adopted. For new disclosures like value-chain emissions, “report or explain” would be better than swinging between mandate and retreat. New mandates could be phased in with a comply-or-explain period, as the bond-borrowing rule was. Hard law should remain for the core: Related-party transactions, audit, minority protection and disclosure of material events.  Explanations need policing too. Britain’s Financial Reporting Council reviews companies’ corporate governance reporting annually and calls out boilerplate explanations. Sebi or the exchanges could do the same, but would need to build the necessary capacity.  Mandatory rules set a floor, and India needs such floors — on board structure, pay, succession and disclosure quality. Investors have a stake. But CSR shows India will mandate when explanations fail. It should be as willing to move the other way when a mandate becomes a ritual. More flexible regulations will help boards move beyond box-ticking towards governing. 
The writer is with Institutional Investors Advisory Services, a Sebi registered proxy advisory firm. The views are personal. @AmitTandon_In     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Budget may stay within deficit goal, but spending plans need realism
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Budget may stay within deficit goal, but spending plans need realismBudget may stay within deficit goal, but spending plans need realism

Worrying about fiscal deficit is fine, but meeting spending targets is more important

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

A K Bhattacharya New Delhi 7 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:49 PM ISTConsultations with stakeholders for the upcoming Union Budget began this week. Fourteen rounds of such discussions will take place until November 26. Perhaps reflecting the political mood, the finance ministry has decided to hold consultations also with GenZ representatives, including students and young professionals. Economists and farm-sector representatives have already urged the finance ministry to stick to its debt reduction goal despite expenditure pressure, review the government’s stance on long-term capital gains tax without necessarily abolishing it only for foreign investors, improve the targeting of fertiliser subsidies, and ease priority-sector lending norms as well as procedures for importing cattle feed ingredients that are in short supply. The Budget exercise has truly begun.  What Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman will present on February 1, 2027, will be her ninth consecutive Union Budget (excluding one interim Budget). Quite apart from the fact that the 2027-28 Budget will make Ms Sitharaman the finance minister to have produced the most Union Budgets, it will also present perhaps her biggest challenge: Maintaining fiscal prudence while propping up the growth engine to benefit all sections of society. Concerns over demand and investments have become as important as the challenges arising from jobs and wages. Official numbers on unemployment show a marginal decline, along with an increase in the labour force participation rate, but real wages have either stagnated or even fallen for a large number of workers in the last decade. External sector problems look a little more manageable with the recent decline in international crude-oil prices, but a widening trade deficit in merchandise goods reflects weaknesses afflicting manufacturing and exporting firms, particularly those in the medium and small sector.    Data for the Union government’s revenue and expenditure during the first half of 2026-27 is available. A look at these numbers points to a few worrying signals. Questions are bound to arise regarding the Union government’s ability to meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.3 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026-27.  Tepid growth in net tax revenue in the first half of the current year at less than 4 per cent is the first cause of concern. The full-year’s net tax revenue growth target was over 9 per cent. Non-tax revenues and miscellaneous non-debt capital receipts (or revenue from disinvestment and asset monetisation) have done well. Non-tax revenues grew by 3 per cent even though the full-year’s projection under this head envisaged no increase, while receipts from disinvestment more than doubled against a much lower target of increasing it by about 35 per cent. However, this is no real comfort. Non-tax revenues and disinvestment receipts account for less than a fifth of the government’s total projected non-debt receipts for 2026-27.  A bigger concern is the pace of expenditure growth in the first half of the current year. Against an annual budgeted target of 9 per cent, the growth in the government’s total expenditure was close to 11 per cent. Growth in revenue expenditure was about 10 per cent, against the annual target of less than 8 per cent, and capital expenditure in the first half of 2026-27 grew by 13 per cent, a shade lower than the annual target of 14 per cent. This is not a healthy sign, particularly when private-sector investments have not yet gained the desired momentum.  The government’s fiscal performance in the first half of 2026-27 reveals yet another problem. At the start of the year, it had announced a brave plan to cut subsidies by about 10 per cent over what was spent in 2025-26, although it was not clear how that reduction would be achieved. Even if there were some plans to cut subsidies, those were dashed about a month after the Budget was presented, when the war in West Asia led to a blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fourth of global crude oil and gas supplies pass.  Not only did international crude-oil prices spike, but even supplies of oil and gas were adversely affected. Fertiliser prices too shot up. This poured cold water on the government’s plans to cut its major subsidies, almost 45 per cent of which are accounted for by fertilisers and petroleum products. Prices of crude oil and fertilisers have now fallen and stabilised. But even before prices came down, the government managed its fertiliser subsidies quite well. In the first half of 2026-27, fertiliser subsidy growth was restricted to 11 per cent (largely due to linking fertiliser sales to farmers’ land holdings with the help of Agristack and other similar digital platforms) and even the growth in the food subsidies bill was reined in at about 17 per cent.    Remember that the petroleum subsidies bill was kept under check because the oil companies absorbed the impact of higher crude-oil prices, helped as they were by the government move to reduce excise duty on petroleum products, mainly petrol and diesel. State-controlled oil companies took a hit as a result, as did the government’s net tax revenues and prospects of dividend income from them. Going forward, this cannot be good news for the Union government’s fiscal consolidation plan.  Already, the government’s fertiliser subsidies bill by the second week of November 2026 has reportedly risen to ₹1.46 trillion, almost 85 per cent of the budgeted allocation under this head for the full year. It is clear that the government’s major subsidies outlay of ₹4.1 trillion will be exceeded by a good margin by the time the current year ends. With net tax revenues growth a little subdued and expenditure slippages almost certain, can the government meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.3 per cent of GDP? To its credit, the government has in the past few years generally refrained from seeking recourse to imaginative accounting techniques, and instead embraced transparent accounting practices. Hopefully, the government will continue to stay on course in this regard. More importantly, however, the government may not be under any pressure to employ such techniques as issuing oil bonds many years ago or tapping extra budgetary resources through fully-serviced government bonds until five years ago. This is because the government’s own ability to spend the resources allocated by it during the year is limited. Over the years, its absorptive capacity to spend the entire money allocated under various important schemes has remained poor. In 2025-26, actual total expenditure by the government was about 3 per cent short of what was budgeted at the start of the year. If a similar saving of 3 per cent is achieved in 2026-27, the government would enjoy an expenditure cushion of about ₹1.6 trillion. This could absorb a good part of the likely revenue shortfall (which will be lower because of a sharp increase in disinvestment receipts) and even the slippage in subsidies expenditure.  Two messages emerge from this. One, the government should not be unduly worried about its performance on the fiscal consolidation front. Even though its revenues do not match up to its targets and subsidies bill exceeds the budgeted amount, it will continue to enjoy the benefit of expenditure savings and keep the fiscal deficit from becoming much wider than the target. Two, while preparing the 2027-28 Budget, it should be more focused on instilling a degree of realism and pragmatism in preparing its expenditure plan. An economy that needs to grow faster requires more investment and proper expenditure planning, particularly in key infrastructure areas.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India's labour Codes at one: From reform to results, what has changed?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's labour Codes at one: From reform to results, what has changed?India's labour Codes at one: From reform to results, what has changed?

India's labour Codes must move from regulatory reform to effective implementation, ensuring better worker protection and ease of doing business

premium

Importantly, the labour Codes lay the foundation for extending social security coverage to unorganised, gig and platform workers (Photo: Shutterstock)

Sumita Dawra5 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:04 PM ISTA year ago, on November 21 2025, the government notified the labour Codes, marking one of India’s most comprehensive labour reforms since Independence. Nearly five years after Parliament passed the Codes in 2019-2020, the government moved towards implementation, having engaged with stakeholders in the intervening period to undertake preparatory work and clarify  key provisions. With the focus now shifting to execution, it is timely to take stock of the progress made during the first year and consider what more needs to be done to ensure that the reforms deliver their intended outcomes.  A significant development, first and foremost, has been the progress towards a common regulatory framework, replacing the complex web of statutes and compliance requirements that historically discouraged business expansion. While addressing stakeholder concerns is an ongoing process, a near-uniform acceptance of the codes is evident.   From notification to operationalisation of rules  Following notification, several procedural and compliance provisions of the Codes required detailed rules. Therefore, the government published the draft Central rules under all four Codes on 30 December 2025, inviting stakeholder comments and suggestions. Following the consultation process, final Central rules under all four Codes were notified in May 2026.  With labour on the concurrent list, states and union territories must also notify rules within their jurisdictions. At the state level, the process of framing and notifying corresponding rules has progressed at varying speeds. While some states and union territories have notified final rules under all four Codes, others are at final stages of rule-making.  Digital compliance and ease of doing business  Digital compliance is a key driver of ease of doing business (EoDB). The labour ministry has launched the revamped Shram Suvidha 2.0 portal in recent months, enabling businesses to obtain a single registration, secure a single licence and file a single return, thereby simplifying compliance across labour authorities.  A pragmatic approach appears to allow states to retain their existing digital compliance systems rather than requiring their integration into a single Central portal. For businesses operating across multiple states, Shram Suvidha is expected to serve as a common interface for coordinated compliance and time-bound approvals.  Building a wider social security ecosystem  Importantly, the labour Codes lay the foundation for extending social security coverage to unorganised, gig and platform workers. In a significant step towards operationalising this framework, the Union government, on 30 October 2026, notified the constitution of two separate National Social Security Boards — one for unorganised workers and the other for gig and platform workers.   The Boards are mandated to recommend, advise on and monitor welfare schemes for these categories of workers, thereby paving the way for more inclusive social security coverage and strengthening the formalisation of India’s workforce. Further, the e-Shram portal’s aggregator module continues to facilitate the registration and integration of platform workers into the social security framework, representing an important dimension of extending social security coverage to the gig and platform economy.  What has changed for workers and businesses?  As implementation progresses, the labour Codes are beginning to deliver tangible benefits for workers and businesses. For workers, a key reform is the uniform definition of wages, establishing a minimum 50 per cent wage base for calculating social security contributions and other statutory benefits. Industry practitioners indicate that most large enterprises have undertaken wage restructuring and made necessary financial provisions.  Two other illustrative indications from the field concern maternity benefits and payment of wages. In both areas, the Codes have expanded the Central government’s jurisdiction. Increased representations reportedly received by Central labour authorities in these areas suggest greater awareness and use of these mechanisms.  Apart from digital compliance mechanisms being in place, the inspector-cum-facilitator system defined under the Codes brings relief to businesses. It seeks to replace the traditional inspection-heavy approach with risk-based oversight, digital reporting and an emphasis on self-compliance.   EPFO reforms and expansion of formal social security  Meanwhile, the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) has strengthened the formal social security framework by notifying its schemes in June 2026. Effective 17 September 2026, the mandatory EPFO wage ceiling also increased from  ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 per month, extending provident fund, pension and insurance coverage to more employees.  Additionally, the VISHWAS and AMNESTY schemes, notified in June 2026, signal a shift towards facilitation rather than enforcement alone.  What stakeholders expect next  Stakeholders may continue to require handholding, clarity and predictability in the implementation process for some time. Key priorities would include timely state-level notifications, effective grievance redressal mechanisms, operationalisation of the floor wage framework, a single point of contact for resolving EPF-related issues, early notification of social security schemes for the unorganised sector, to name a few.   Representatives of the construction industry have suggested an integrated labour database or a ‘labour stack’ that could play a critical role in enabling portability of benefits, ensuring continuity of coverage and preventing duplication.  The road ahead: From reform to delivery  Ultimately, the Codes’ success will be measured by outcomes, some of these being: Wage related, greater female labour force participation, safer workplaces, greater formalisation of India’s labour market, a predictable compliance environment with enhanced transparency and simplification of processes for greater EoDB.

entry.title: The Tata group & national security: Why resolving internal disputes matters
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The Tata group & national security: Why resolving internal disputes mattersThe Tata group & national security: Why resolving internal disputes matters

Tata Group's internal disputes must be resolved peacefully to protect its legacy and India's national interests

premium

The Tata group is trusted by the people, something which cannot be said of the private sector generally (Photo: Shutterstock)

Tarun Das5 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTIndia and the world have been witness to an unseemly campaign and warfare in the Tata group over the last few months. Unprecedented in their history.  What is the Tata group all about? Is it just another private sector company? Or, is it the icon of Indian industry? Is its leadership expected to be nation- oriented? What is the nature of the expectation of the country and our people about the Tata group? Perhaps, the answers are obvious.  Since Jamsetji Tata set up Tata Steel in Jamshedpur and J R D Tata expanded to new areas of industrial activity, Ratan Tata, over a 30-year period took the group global, acquiring the UK’s Corus Steel and Jaguar Land Rover, two particular examples. On the night of the final bidding for Corus Steel, and as Ratan Tata, B Muthuraman (MD, Tata Steel), and others were entering the bidding room, Ratan famously said that he will bid high to acquire Corus Steel against Brazilian competition because this acquisition was not just about Tata — it was about India and its global image.  Here are some more examples:First, the setting up of cancer hospitals around the country to bring cancer treatment nearer to those in need of care.  Second, massive investment in semiconductors in Gujarat and Assam, to build India’s technological strength.  Third, the acquisition of Air India, sick and struggling, so that it remained India’s national airline.  Fourth, Tata Nano, a ₹1 lakh car project built for the common people of India, so that they could afford a car.  Fifth, the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bengaluru, which was founded by the Tatas.  Again and again, the Tata group has served the nation. In the process, it has become a public service industry institution, a national asset and a symbol of national security. The 26/11 terrorist attack on the Taj Mahal Hotel in Mumbai is a reminder that Tata is a target when India is to be wounded.  In fact, these characteristics of the Tata group make it essential for the Prime Minister, the Home Minister and the National Security Adviser to be the ultimate deciding authorities because national security is in their hands.  The Tata group is trusted by the people, something which cannot be said of the private sector generally.  It is India’s icon, respected and admired across the country, and the world.  Its majority shareholding has historically been with Tata Trusts and there has never been a problem till very recently.  The recent public media coverage has been damaging to the Tata group’s image and reputation, and has disturbed its employees and customers, as well as the public at large and, surely, the government and its various agencies.  In reality, the Tata group is about India: It is the industrial backbone of India, the Industrial culture of India, the industrial potential of India, the Industrial technology of India, the industrial growth of India.  More than that, it’s about the people of India. Tata belongs to India. Tata is India. Tata must remain true to its original identity. Tata is not a plaything of a few individuals, it can never be.  The ongoing publicity about internal differences is deeply damaging to the Tata name and to India.  One cannot help but recall the many instances of corporate groups splitting, dividing, breaking up — some with much unseemly publicity and some quietly, with dignity.   One recent example was the Godrej group which did it with dignity and self-respect. Both sides appointed the finest experts: Nimesh Kampani and AZB Partners to represent the Jamshyd Godrej side and Uday Kotak with Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas on the Adi Godrej side. Perhaps, there is a lesson here for people involved with the Tata group. It took time, it took patience but, eventually, the settlement was completed without public acrimony.   This could be a pathway for the leadership of Tata Trusts and Tata Sons, recalling the words of the Prime Minister in another context, that “this is not the time for war, this is a time for dialogue and diplomacy”. If the people concerned do not follow the direction shown by the Prime Minister to countries which are at war, then the government has enormous powers and a variety of instruments to bring peace, as it must in the national security interest of the country.  This has been an unfortunate year in the long history of the Tata group. The next year must show that a new pathway of peace is the way forward, either through voluntary internal dialogue or through government action. The national security interests of the country have to be given overriding importance. The Tata group is very much part of India’s national security.

entry.title: RBI may need tighter monetary policy to contain persistent inflation
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI may need tighter monetary policy to contain persistent inflationRBI may need tighter monetary policy to contain persistent inflation

Its decision to look through successive supply shocks could prove costly

premium

Rajeswari Sengupta5 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:46 PM ISTIndia’s retail inflation rose to 6.09 per cent in October, crossing the upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India’s tolerance band for the first time in two years. This wasn’t unexpected. Over the last few months, food prices have been going up, energy costs have increased and inflationary pressures have been getting more generalised, beyond just food and energy. The RBI’s response so far has been one repo rate hike of 25 basis points in October. It is worth asking, has the RBI fallen behind the curve?  Let’s review the facts first. Inflation did not jump overnight. It has been steadily rising since January and crossed the RBI’s 4 per cent target in June. Core inflation, which leaves out food and fuel, has also been going up. It has increased from 3.3 per cent in January to 4.6 per cent in October. According to the latest data, inflation rose in 11 of the 12 groups of the consumer price index. The pressure is no longer limited to a few items.  Three factors are responsible for this.  First, food inflation has more than doubled from 4 per cent in April to 8.5 per cent in October. El Nino conditions meant that India received only 87 per cent of its long-term average rainfall during the June-September monsoon season, the lowest since 2015. Deficient rainfall has affected the kharif (summer) crop and also the reservoir levels, raising concerns about the ongoing rabi (winter) crop output too.  Second, the war in West Asia has pushed up prices of crude oil and gas. The Indian government raised petrol and diesel prices by about 8 per cent. Prices of commercial LPG and other inputs such as chemicals and plastics went up by more. Wholesale inflation averaged 10.4 per cent in the July-September quarter. Over time, firms pass on higher input costs to consumers. Higher energy prices also pushed up transport inflation from nearly 0 per cent in April to 5.8 per cent in October.  Third, there is a demand dimension.  If official data is to be believed, real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 7.8 per cent in April-June. Non-food bank credit grew at a staggering rate of 19 per cent in September. Personal loans from banks grew 17.3 per cent, against 11.5 per cent a year ago while retail loans from non-banking finance companies (NBFCs) grew 21.9 per cent. Households are borrowing to spend. This suggests that we have an economy that is growing at close to 8 per cent, where credit-fuelled consumption is pushing up demand, and that has faced two supply shocks in one year — an energy shock and a food shock.  Now let’s look at the RBI’s monetary policy conduct against this background.  These risks were visible well before October. The RBI itself flagged the oil shock and the El Niño risk in its April policy. But it kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent in its April, June and August meetings. It raised the rate to 5.5 per cent in October. That hike only reversed the cut of December 2025.  In fact, in its August meeting, the RBI lowered its inflation forecast for the year to 5 per cent, even though inflation was rising every month. The August meeting was interesting for another reason. The minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee meeting revealed that some members were concerned about persistent inflationary pressures, strong credit growth and rising inflation expectations of households. But, the monetary policy statement published by the RBI came across as more dovish. This suggests that the RBI did not give sufficient weight to the possibility that persistent food and energy shocks would spread to other prices.  The result is that with a repo rate of 5.5 per cent and a headline CPI inflation of 6.09 per cent, the real rate is roughly -0.6 per cent. This means that monetary policy needs to be sufficiently more contractionary in order to bring inflation down to the target level of 4 per cent.  The RBI’s reasoning may be that supply shocks are temporary and a central bank should look through them. This holds when it is a one-time shock, demand is weak and expectations are stable. It is harder to defend when two supply shocks come together, growth is strong, credit is growing at 19 per cent and core inflation is rising. In such conditions, supply shocks spread to wages and other prices. While monetary policy cannot produce more rainfall or lower global oil prices, it can play a crucial role in preventing a supply shock from becoming a persistent inflation problem.  Why does this matter? It matters because inflation is a tax on households. It hurts the poor and the middle class the most. The inflation targeting framework was adopted in 2016 to avoid such episodes. Also, there is a cost to waiting. Once households start revising their inflation expectations upwards, bringing inflation down becomes harder. The RBI may now have to raise rates by more, and keep them higher for longer, to lower both inflation and inflation expectations but at a greater cost to growth.  Hopefully, the central bank would take decisive action going forward to halt the steady rise in inflation and bring it back to the 4 per cent target.  
The writer is associate professor of economics, Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, Mumbai     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Abolish B schools vs pivot B schools? Time to focus on entrepreneurship
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Abolish B schools vs pivot B schools? Time to focus on entrepreneurshipAbolish B schools vs pivot B schools? Time to focus on entrepreneurship

Rather than shutting down, Indian B-schools must pivot from producing corporate talent to nurturing entrepreneurs and future business leaders

premium

Students attending a management class at a business school in India

Ambi Parameswaran5 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:34 PM ISTEver since the article with a sensational title “Should we shut down B Schools” appeared in The New York Times, there has been renewed debate about all that is wrong with business school education. The article was written by Chris Marquis of Cambridge University’s Judge Business School. Marquis has over two decades of experience as a tenured B School professor. If he is calling for a ‘shut down’, there must be some truth to his argument, feel a lot of people.   In India, too, there has been a debate around B schools. Tulsi Jayakumar, a professor at SPJIMR (S P Jain Institute of Management and Research) has argued in her op-ed piece in The Times Of India (November 13, 2026) that Indian B schools are caught in a trap of placement and rankings. Rankings are driven by research and a lot of the research output stays in an echo chamber. The case-method of education pioneered by the Harvard Business School (borrowing the idea from the Harvard Law School, if I may add) has also come in for criticism.   One of the big complaints by Marquis is that B Schools are producing graduates who are single mindedly focused on profit maximisation. And repaying their own student loans. The preferred job options are in consulting and financial services. Very few enter the manufacturing or services sector, even fewer the non-profit sector. The need to bring a stronger societal-well-being focus was also one of the arguments that we have read in the book Rethinking The MBA  (2010, Harvard Business Review Press) written by Srikant Datar, David Garvin and Patrick Cullen.   Let us now switch tracks and look at the Indian scenario. We have over 5,000-plus B schools in India. All B schools that fall below the 200-ranking mark, whichever ranking you may take, are struggling. Enrollments are a challenge. And placements are a bigger challenge. For the top ten or so schools the scenario that was presented by Marquis is similar. Students prefer to join consulting or financial services.   I discussed this with a few students whom I had lunch with before my session at a leading B school just before Diwali. They were curious to know how I jumped into a relatively unknown sector (advertising) after my Indian Institute of Management (IIM)  education.  Was it just foolhardiness or did I really think that through?   I explained that my reason was simple. I had done a summer internship with the ad agency and thought they offered a great learning environment. While the salary was not great, I knew that I would be able to get a significant jump if I proved my mettle. Also as an MBA from a leading business school I was quite sure that I would be able to pivot after a year or two.   How about them? Why this craze to chase the biggest pay packet? Their argument was that many of their friends had big student loans to clear. The easy route to clear those loans was to grab the biggest pay packet. They felt that many of their friends will jump out in two or three years; to head to a sector that interests them. What could they be? A start-up that can help them on their own entrepreneurial journey, was the answer.   That got me thinking.   In 1979 I  joined an ad agency that was started by two MBA graduates, one from Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad (IIMA) and one from Indian Institute of Management  Calcutta (IIMC). It was a start-up, although you may not have used the term then.   And later in my career I went back into advertising, after a nine-year stint in marketing/sales. My entry into advertising was also in a quasi-entrepreneurial role. I was part of a team of five MBAs who came together to turn around an ailing ad agency. It was as entrepreneurial as you can get. We did succeed in saving jobs and turning the agency around; we even managed to find a global buyer for an agency that was said to be on its deathbed just a decade earlier.   This leads me to an argument that is missing from all these ‘shut down B school’ sloganeering. In a country like India we need new companies with growth ambitions. B schools are tailor-made to teach young bright students how to set up and run a business. No other form of education — Bachelor of Commerce (B Com), engineering, Chartered Accountant (CA) or law — comes close.   B schools need to pivot. From being providers of talent to consultancies and financial service majors to creators of future entrepreneurs. Towards this end they should add new courses, new programmes. For example the family managed business programmes offered by several B schools serve a great cause. They try and teach the future inheritors the way to grow their businesses. Then there are online MBA programmes that attract young leaders who are building their own businesses.   As Jayakumar has said in her article, B schools should track their alumni through their career journey. Maybe bring them back for refreshers. Find out how many of them are in entrepreneurial roles or quasi-entrepreneurial roles. There is no point in condemning the craze for consulting or financial services. They pay the most, so let them get the choicest of candidates. But tracking the alumni in a systematic way will definitely help the B school serve the larger cause.   So instead of shutting down B schools, we should ask them to use a term popularised by start-ups: Pivot. By becoming schools for entrepreneurs.  
The writer is an adjunct professor of marketing at SPJIMR, a  best-selling author and founder of Brand-Building.com, a brand advisory   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
